title: Regulated Unproductive Splicing in Animal Development
text:
Poison Exons (PEs) are important in development and their dysregulation causes several human diseases. The
proposed study aims to identify novel PEs using long read sequencing, perform targeted disruption of PEs to
determine their functional role in regulating vertebrate development, and investigate the mechanism of gene
regulation by PEs. Results from this study may provide insights into developmental disorders and advance
potential therapeutic interventions.

title: Monitoring CAR T Cell Therapeutic Response and Toxicity with Real-time, Label-free Cell Quantification
text:
This project aims to develop a rapid, label-free, and cost-effective method for patient blood Chimeric Antigen
Receptor (CAR) T cell quantification combining surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy and machine learning.
The application of this method in the unmet need for point-of-care CAR T cell counting will provide input on
therapeutic efficacy and critically indicate signs of toxicity to overall improve patient outcomes for this
treatment. In both the short and long term, the proposed research promises to provide new insights into CAR T
cell mechanisms as well as to enhance the development of safer and more effective CAR therapies.

title: The role of MAB-5, a Hox transcription factor, in establishing and maintaining neuronal identity and connectivity
text:
Neuronal cell identity must be appropriately established and maintained throughout life for
proper function. This proposal is aimed at understanding the role of the transcription factor
MAB-5 (ANTP/HOX6-8) in establishing and maintaining differences in gene transcription and
synaptic connectivity in the model organism nematode C. elegans. This work is designed to
contribute to foundational knowledge of nervous system development.

title: Loss of Conserved Regulatory Elements in Human Brain Evolution
text:
This research investigates how the loss of deeply conserved gene regulatory elements shaped human brain
evolution and contributes to neurological disorders such as autism and epilepsy. By integrating evolutionary
genomics, high-throughput functional assays, and human genetic data, the project will identify regulatory variants
that alter brain development. Understanding these mechanisms will improve interpretation of non-coding variants
in clinical sequencing and advance precision diagnostics for neurological diseases.

title: Proline tRNA biogenesis as oncogenic drivers and therapeutic target in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it seeks to dissect mechanisms by which
deregulation of tRNA biogenesis rewires gene expression and contributes to T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
(T-ALL). Relapsed/refractory T-ALL is associated with dismal survival rate of less than 25%. The proposed
research is relevant to NIH’s mission as it paves the way for the development of novel cancer therapeutics
focused on targeting tRNA regulatory pathways in T-ALL and potentially other cancers.

title: Efficient IBD mapping for Alzheimer's Disease and related brain imaging phenotypes
text:
Identical-by-descent segments inferred from genome-wide data provide information on population history and
genetic relatedness that are not sufficiently used in current genetic association approaches. We propose to
leverage identical-by-descent segments in the genetic association mapping for Alzheimer’s Disease and related
brain imaging endophenotypes, develop efficient statistical methods and implement novel computational
algorithms that can be applied to large samples. Our tools and findings will facilitate genetic research and provide
novel insights into the genetic architecture of Alzheimer’s Disease.

title: Study of a new driver and therapeutic vulnerability of bone metastasis
text:
Understanding and targeting the molecular underpinnings of bone metastasis remains one of the most pressing
challenges in cancer treatment. Our discovery of ACBP as a previously undescribed bone metastasis driver
demonstrates the power of in vivo forward genetics screening and uncovers the pivotal role of lipid metabolism
in tumor cell adaptation to and thriving in the bone microenvironment. The successful completion of this project
will reveal novel targets for the treatment of bone metastases.

title: Transcriptional Regulation of CD4+ T Cell Differentiation and Diversified Memory
text:
CD4+ T cell differentiation has a big impact on both cellular and humoral immune responses. Memory
T cell formation is also the scientific basis for the development of many vaccines. Our proposal to
understand CD4+ T cell differentiation and memory will provide important knowledge on how to control
infectious diseases, autoimmune disorders, and to aid vaccine development for new pandemic
threats.

title: Multi-level drivers of cardiovascular health during cancer survivorship
text: Americans with cancer have more than twice the risk of poor cardiovascular disease (CVD) outcomes compared to those without cancer; and we hypothesize that upstream, area-level factors and individual-level socio-economic position are partially responsible for this difference. The goal of this proposed R01 application is to elucidate the role of multi-level drivers of poor CVD outcomes among a large, community-based cohort of nearly 8,000 adults diagnosed with cancer. Our proposed work will generate new evidence to inform targeted interventions designed to prevent poor CVD outcomes during cancer survivorship.

title: VA RR&D Center for Neurorestoration and Neurotechnology
text:
Disorders of the brain and nervous system, including those resulting directly from injuries incurred
during military service, are of immediate relevance to Veterans Health. In part because of the complexity
of the nervous system, people who have disorders such as spinal cord injury, stroke, post-traumatic
stress disorder, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or limb loss lack adequate rehabilitation therapies to
regain their independence. Through rigorous translational and clinical research conducted by a
multidisciplinary team of scientists, engineers, and clinicians, the VA RR&D Center for Neurorestoration
and Neurotechnology develops and tests novel device-based approaches to improving the health and
lives of Veterans. An explicit goal of the Center is to translate neurotechnology and its applications into
clinical practice in service to our Veterans and civilians throughout the US.

title: Quantitative Mechanoporation for High Throughput Cell Surgery
text:
The permeability of cell membranes can increase significantly when they are stretched, however the specific
underlying mechanisms remains poorly understood. The objective of this work is to uncover how pores are
created by stretching cell membranes, by characterizing the dynamic structure and permeability of these pores
using new microfluidic and optical nano-imaging technologies. This knowledge will be valuable for developing
better methods of delivering therapeutic genes, drugs, and nanoparticles into cells.

title: Epstein-Barr virus molecular pathogenesis in the nasopharynx and the role of LMP1 in lytic infection
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a ubiquitous gamma-herpesvirus associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), which has an estimated global cancer burden of ~78,000 cases per year. On average, more than 90% of adults worldwide are seropositive but control of the latent and lytic infection cycles is paramount to EBV pathogenesis in the nasopharynx. This proposal seeks to redefine the EBV principal oncoprotein, latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), as a virulence factor that facilitates the induction of the lytic cascade.

title: Emerging Strategies for Therapy of Metastatic Brain Cancer
text:
Brain cancer is a leading cause of death and brain metastases represent a highly unmet clinical need.
In particular, brain metastases from breast cancer are associated with dismal prognosis. This proposal seeks to
elucidate the mechanisms by which breast cancer spreads to the brain, utilizing our in vivo models to evaluate
brain tumor tropic genes, novel imaging methods of cellular tracking in the CNS, and ultimately development of
a novel stem cell-based therapy for HER2+ brain metastases.

title: Mitochondrial Calcium Uniporter in Signaling and Dynamics
text: The proteins mediating mitochondrial calcium uptake have been identified but many of their roles in calcium transport and beyond remain an enigma. We will test if the MICU regulators of calcium uptake are important for individual cells’ calcium signal fingerprints, for redox homeostasis and for fusion-fission and cristae dynamics of the mitochondria. These studies will inform on the pathways by which MICUs support mitochondrial structure, dynamics and signaling, and on the pathogenesis initiated by their perturbations.

title: Michigan State University VDL VetLRN 2022
text:
Microbial or chemical contamination of food or drugs poses a significant risk to both public and animal health
and the laboratory testing supported by the Vet-LIRN program creates a mechanism for early detection of
contaminated or adulterated animal feed or drugs. The network provides support for the required response
capacity in the event of food- or drug- related animal injury or illness. Vet-LIRN directly supports national
food safety and security through established protocols that coordinate efficient reporting to FDA and ensure
a process to support rapid notification of appropriate public or animal health officials in a case of an
emergency.

title: Eicosanoid Pathways Underlying Disease Risk in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
text:
Despite advances in the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension, morbidity and mortality
remain unacceptably high. To improve our currently limited understanding of how complex bioactive metabolite
pathways interact to promote or prevent pulmonary hypertension, we will study upstream mediators of
endothelial dysfunction in relation to disease risk and progression, in comprehensive study design. These studies
can identify novel pathogenic and prognostic biomarkers and future therapeutic interventions.

title: High-Throughput Functional Genomics of Variants in Genes Linked to Substance Use Disorders
text:
The research proposed in this application will advance the genetics of addiction by using innovative technology
to provide experimental measurement of the consequences of thousands of genetics variants in regions of the
human genome that code for proteins, as well as those regions that turn genes on and off. By contributing
significantly to an understanding of the molecular contributions to addiction, this work will enable future
development of treatments that directly target its underlying biological basis.

title: Structural Basis of Nociceptor Channel TRPM3 gating and pharmacology
text:
TRPM3, a calcium-permeable nonselective cation channel, plays a key role in pain perception in somatosensory
neurons, and inhibition of TRPM3 in pain models showed analgesic effects in mice, highlighting TRPM3 as a
potential target for novel pain medications. This research project will focus on determining the first molecular
structures of TRPM3 and elucidating the gating mechanism and pharmacology, taking advantage of single-
particle cryo-EM and electrophysiological recording. The proposed research is relevant to public health and NIH’s
mission, because the work will provide a deep understanding and knowledge of the relationships between atomic
structure, function, and pharmacology of the nociceptor channel TRPM3, as well as a foundation for developing
new drugs for the treatment of chronic pain.

title: Dissecting high-risk cell states in neuroblastoma
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because the discovery of vulnerabilities in the chemoresistant
cell states found at tumor relapse is expected to lead to the development of more effective approaches to therapy
in these high-risk states. Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the NCI mission of advancing fundamental
knowledge to enhance health and reduce illness and disability from cancer.

title: Discovery and characterization of clinically actionable germline mutations in DNA damage repair (DDR) pathway genes in lung cancer
text:
The proposed study will provide an evidence for the contribution of inherited mutations in DNA damage
repair (DDR) genes in lung cancer susceptibility and etiology. It has immediate translational and preventive
implications as lung cancer patients with DDR abnormalities would benefit from targeted therapies, such as
PARP inhibitors and the genetic testing offered to undiagnosed relatives (cascade testing) would identify
high-risk individuals for earlier or more frequent low doze CT screening for early detection.
